2 Disease Testing using Bayesian Methods

2.1 Testing for Covid-19

Motivating Example 1: Covid-19 Disease Test

  • •

    A new test for Covid-19 has been developed.

  • •

    It is fast and cheap, but has moderate accuracy.

  • •

    It has been tested on a limited sample of people with known Covid status.

  • •

    You are selected at random from the UK population in August 2020 and you test positive, what is the probability that you have Covid-19?

  • •

    If instead you were selected at random from the London population in Jan 2021, what is the probability then?

  • •

    The following data show the limited sample of 620 hospital patients (the test group) used for a trial of the new test. They are classified according to the presence or absence of Covid-19 (as diagnosed by a “gold standard”) and the results of the new test.

Has Covid-19?
Yes No Total
D+ D−
Test result positive T+ 209 6 215
Test result negative T− 11 394 405
Total 220 400 620

Notation and Terminology

  • •

    Suppose that a person may or may not have a disease, and a test for this disease is available. We denote the various events for this problem as follows:

    D+ = person has disease
    D− = person does not have disease
    T+ = person tests positive for disease
    T− = person tests negative for disease

  • •

    We need to distinguish between the probability distribution of the test group (e.g. in the case of the example above, those 620 patients that were tested) and the probability distribution of the general population — i.e. the group from which we sampled the person about whom we want to know whether they have the disease or not:

    Pt = probability distribution for the test group
    P = probability distribution of the general population

  • •

    The sensitivity of a test is the conditional probability that the patient tests positive, given that the patient has the disease, Pt⁢(T+|D+).

  • •

    The specificity of a test is the conditional probability that the patient tests negative, given that the patient does not have the disease, Pt⁢(T−|D−).

  • •

    There are two incorrect results: Pt⁢(T+|D−) is a false positive and Pt⁢(T−|D+) is a false negative. Often, the latter is more important. Balancing the two rests on clinical judgements.

Summary of definitions: events, distributions and probabilities

  • ∗

    Events:

    • ∙

      D+ = person has disease

    • ∙

      D− = person does not have disease

    • ∙

      T+ = person tests positive for disease

    • ∙

      T− = person tests negative for disease

  • ∗

    Probability Distributions (note the distinction):

    • ∙

      Pt = probability distribution for the test group (sample)

    • ∙

      P = probability distribution of the general population

  • ∗

    Probabilities:

    • ∙

      Pt⁢(T+|D+) = sensitivity of the test

    • ∙

      Pt⁢(T−|D−) = specificity of the test

    • ∙

      Pt⁢(T+|D−) = probability of false positive

    • ∙

      Pt⁢(T−|D+) = probability of false negative (often more important)

Covid-19 Disease Test Example Continued

  • •

    Sensitivity: Pt⁢(T+|D+)=Pt⁢(T+∩D+)Pt⁢(D+)=(209620)(220620)=209220=0.95

  • •

    Specificity: Pt⁢(T−|D−)=Pt⁢(T−∩D−)Pt⁢(D−)=(394620)(400620)=394400=0.985

  • •

    False positive: Pt⁢(T+|D−)=1−Pt⁢(T−|D−)=1−0.985=0.015

  • •

    False negative: Pt⁢(T−|D+)=1−Pt⁢(T+|D+)=1−0.95=0.05

We note that actually this test seems to be pretty accurate.

Question

If we classify patients for Covid-19 from the general UK population with, among other things, a very different ratio of people who have the disease to that of the test group, will these four conditional probabilities differ substantially?

  • •

    In order for the given data to be useful to make inferences about people tested from the general population, we make the following crucial assumption:

The sensitivity and specificity are a property of the test only

  • and in particular they do not depend on the underlying prevalence of the disease in the underlying test group. Hence, in particular:

    Pt⁢(T+|D+) = P⁢(T+|D+)
    Pt⁢(T−|D−) = P⁢(T−|D−)
    Pt⁢(T+|D−) = P⁢(T+|D−) (3)
    Pt⁢(T−|D+) = P⁢(T−|D+)
  • •

    Note that no other relationship generally holds between Pt and P, for example,

    Pt⁢(D+)≠P⁢(D+) (4)

    in general.

  • •

    Note also that we are neglecting errors due to the limited size of the test group (more on this later in the course).

2.2 Bayesian Inference: from Prior to Posterior

  • •

    For interpreting a diagnostic test, we typically have a prior probability of disease, P⁢(D+). This is usually the background prevalence of disease in the population.

  • •

    From clinical trials (such as in the Covid-19 example given), we can infer also the probability of a particular test outcome given whether a person had the disease or not: this is called the likelihood. Note that the previous assumptions, given by Equations (3), can be restated as: the likelihood of our test does not depend on the general population, but only on test itself.11 1 Whilst the assumptions made in Equation (3) are often reasonable, can you think of a reason why they might be violated?

  • •

    Given further information, such as a positive test result T+, we may be able to calculate a probability which takes into account the information, namely P⁢(D+|T+). We call this the posterior probability of disease given a positive test result.

  • •

    Posterior probabilities must always be reported so that it is clear what the extra information is: P⁢(D+|T−) is the posterior probability of disease (D+) given a negative test result (T−).

Definiton: Summary of prior, likelihood and posterior.

  • •

    P⁢(D+) = prior probability of disease (prevalence in relevant population)

  • •

    P⁢(T+|D+) and P⁢(T+|D−) = likelihood of positive test given disease status

  • •

    P⁢(D+|T+) = posterior probability of disease given positive test

  • •

    Bayes theorem can be used to calculate the posterior probability of disease D+ given the positive test result T+:

    P⁢(D+|T+) =P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)P⁢(T+) (by Bayes Thm.)
    =P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)+P⁢(T+|D−)⁢P⁢(D−) (by Partition Thm.)
    =Pt⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)Pt⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)+Pt⁢(T+|D−)⁢P⁢(D−) (by Test assumption)
  • •

    This shows that the predictive value of a positive test depends on:

    • –

      P⁢(T+|D+) and P⁢(T+|D−), i.e. the likelihood, which depends in turn on the accuracy of the test only.

    • –

      P⁢(D+) and P⁢(D−), the prior probabilities of having/not having the disease, which depend only on the population from which the person was sampled.

  • •

    Important! Note that the denominator used in Bayes Theorem is P⁢(T+)≠Pt⁢(T+), as the test group has a far higher proportion of people with Covid-19 than the UK population, so we could NOT have read this value off from the table of test results (a common mistake).

  • •

    Often both P and Pt are denoted by P, which can lead to confusion.

Covid-19 Test Example: Applying Bayes Theorem (UK Aug 2020 case)

We are finally ready to answer our key question:

“You are selected at random from the UK population in August 2020 and you test positive, what is the probability that you have Covid-19?”

  • •

    In August 2020 it was thought that 0.00025 of the UK population currently had Covid-19. This provides our prior probability of having the disease P⁢(D+).

  • •

    We therefore have that:

    P⁢(D+) =0.00025
    P⁢(T+|D+) =0.95
    P⁢(T−|D−) =0.985
    P⁢(T+|D−) =0.015
    P⁢(T−|D+) =0.05
  • •

    We want to find P⁢(D+|T+), so use Bayes Theorem as described above, and use the fact that P⁢(D−)=1−P⁢(D+):

    P⁢(D+|T+) = P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)+P⁢(T+|D−)⁢P⁢(D−)
    = 0.95×0.000250.95×0.00025+0.015×(1−0.00025)
    = 0.00023750.0002375+0.01499625
    = 0.00023750.04305
    = 0.0156(to 3 s.f)
  • •

    So even given a positive test result from a relatively accurate test, you still only have a 1.56% chance of actually having Covid-19(!).

Discussion: Why is the Posterior probability P⁢(D+|T+) still so low?

  • •

    This probability P⁢(D+|T+)=0.0156 is still pretty low, despite using an accurate test, so what went wrong?

  • •

    It is because our prior probability P⁢(D+)=0.00025 was so low, that although the evidence from T+ increases our probability, it still ends up being relatively small.

  • •

    Another way to see this is if we examine the denominator of Bayes Theorem, which gives us the probability of a positive test result T+. We see that a positive test comes about from two routes: either you had the disease D+ or you did not D−:

    P⁢(T+) = P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)+P⁢(T+|D−)⁢P⁢(D−)
    = 0.0002375+0.01499625
  • •

    We see that the contribution to P⁢(T+) from the D+ route, which is given by the first term on the right hand side, is much smaller than the contribution to P⁢(T+) from the D− route, given by the second term.

  • •

    This means that the majority of people (chosen at random) who would test positive in August 2020 would do so through the D− route, that is because of false positives, and very few, in fact precisely 1.56%, would do so due to true positives.

Covid-19 Test Example: Applying Bayes Theorem (London Jan 2021 case)

If the above discussion is correct, then we should see quite a different result for our second question:

“If instead you were selected at random from the London population in Jan 2021 (and you test positive), what is the probability (that you have Covid-19) then?”

  • •

    In early Jan 2021 it is thought that 0.03 of the London population currently had Covid-19. A similar application of Bayes theorem, but now using the much larger prior probability of P⁢(D+)=0.03, yields:

    P⁢(D+|T+) = P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)+P⁢(T+|D−)⁢P⁢(D−)
    = 0.95×0.030.95×0.03+0.015×(1−0.03)
    = 0.02850.0285+0.01455
    = 0.662(to 3 s.f)
  • •

    So given a positive test result, you now have a 66.2% chance of having Covid-19: a much higher value than before (and much more worrying!).

  • •

    Note: the D+ route contribution in the denominator of Bayes theorem is now significantly higher than the D− route.

  • •

    These two example calculations show that disease tests cannot be evaluated in isolation: the context in which they are applied is very important.

  • •

    The August 2020 example shows the challenges with wide-scale screening (where you test everyone): for rare diseases you may get far more false positives than true positives. This may still be beneficial though, if the disease is considered severe.

2.3 More Advanced Bayesian Calculations

The use of Bayes theorem can be thought of as the simplest procedure in Bayesian statistics, as it just applies to the probability of a yes/no event. However, even in this simple case there is a rich set of calculations we can do.

a) Performing Further Tests

  • •

    Consider the August 2020 UK example above. You had tested positive but still had only a 1.56% chance of having Covid-19. In this case one natural option is to take the test again. You do this and you receive a second positive test, what is your probability now?

  • •

    We denote two positive tests as T++, but now have to consider the nature of the test further.

  • •

    One possible assumption is that the test results are conditionally independent given disease status, implying that

    P⁢(T++|D+)=P⁢(T+|D+)2andP⁢(T++|D−)=P⁢(T+|D−)2 (5)
  • •

    This might be reasonable if the test fails independently each time, i.e. due to reasons entirely unrelated to the specific attributes of the patient.

Covid-19 Test Example: Two Independent Positive Test Results

  • •

    We are in the Aug 2020 UK example and assume the same prior as before: P⁢(D+)=0.00025.

  • •

    But now we want the probability of Covid-19 given two positive test results T++:

    P⁢(D+|T++) = P⁢(T++|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)P⁢(T++|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)+P⁢(T++|D−)⁢P⁢(D−)
    = P⁢(T+|D+)2⁢P⁢(D+)P⁢(T+|D+)2⁢P⁢(D+)+P⁢(T+|D−)2⁢P⁢(D−)
    = 0.952×0.000250.952×0.00025+0.0152×(1−0.00025)
    = 0.501(to 3 s.f)
  • •

    So, under the conditional independence assumption, your posterior probability after two tests is now 50.1%: much higher than the 1.56% from a single positive test.

  • •

    Exercise: check that for the Jan 2021 London scenario, two positive tests would give your posterior to be P⁢(D+|T++)=0.992.

  • •

    Note that independence of test results may not be a reasonable assumption. The other extreme is that the test fails precisely due to specifics of the patient, and will fail in the same way again and again, leading to P⁢(T++|D+)=P⁢(T+|D+). In this case, our posterior probability would remain at 1.56%.

b) A Model for Sequential Learning

  • •

    It is worth pausing to consider the sequential learning that occurs when we do two tests in a row.

  • •

    When we calculated the two test result case we went straight from

    P⁢(D+) ⟶ P⁢(D+|T++)
    0.00025 ⟶   0.501
  • •

    What if instead we update by the first positive test T1+ (occurring on day 1) and then the second positive test T2+ (occurring on day 2)? This is the more natural way of thinking about the data coming in.

  • •

    Well, after seeing a single positive result T1+ we updated to get posterior P⁢(D+|T1+), and trivially also P⁢(D−|T1+). We could then treat these posteriors as our priors for day 2. This means on day 2 we could update using the second positive test T2+ using Bayes theorem (with T++={T1+,T2+}) to get:

P⁢(D+|T++)=P⁢(D+|T1+,T2+)
= P⁢(T2+|D+,T1+)⁢P⁢(D+|T1+)P⁢(T2+|D+,T1+)⁢P⁢(D+|T1+)+P⁢(T2+|D−,T1+)⁢P⁢(D−|T1+)
= P⁢(T2+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+|T1+)P⁢(T2+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+|T1+)+P⁢(T2+|D−)⁢P⁢(D−|T1+)
= 0.95×0.01560.95×0.0156+0.015×0.9844= 0.501

where we have used the assumption regarding conditional independence of T1+ and T2+ (given D+) to simplify terms such as P⁢(T2+|D+,T1+)=P⁢(T2+|D+).

  • •

    Therefore, receiving one positive result, then a second, we have (in the independent tests case):

    P⁢(D+) ⟶ P⁢(D+|T+)⟶P⁢(D+|T++)
    0.00025 ⟶     0.0156⟶        0.501

    that is, as more information comes in, we update our beliefs about the probability of D+ again and again.

  • •

    This final result is the same as going straight from

    P⁢(D+) ⟶ P⁢(D+|T++)
    0.00025 ⟶   0.501

    as in the two test result case.

  • •

    Important! Bayes theorem (and Bayesian statistics) is consistent in the sense that we can update sequentially by one T+ then by another T+, or all at once (i.e. by T++) and we are guaranteed to obtain the same result.

  • •

    This structure motivates the Bayesian mantra: today’s posterior is tomorrow’s prior.

  • •

    Exercise: check the sequential formula for P⁢(D+|T++) for the January 2021 case.

c) Sensitivity of the Posterior P⁢(D+|T+) to the Prior P⁢(D+)

  • •

    The Aug 2020 and Jan 2021 examples showed us that the posterior P⁢(D+|T+) is, in some cases, sensitive to the value of the prior probability.

  • •

    We can explore this locally (for a particular prior specification) by for example, examining the derivative of the posterior with respect to the prior: d⁢P⁢(D+|T+)/d⁢P⁢(D+).

  • •

    If we are somewhat unsure of the prior probability, but would take a certain action (e.g. self-isolation) if the posterior P⁢(D+|T+) is over a certain threshold (and take no action if it is below), we can rearrange Bayes theorem to solve for P⁢(D+) in terms of the posterior P⁢(D+|T+): see Question 5 on the problem sheets.

  • •

    This will inform us of the threshold of how high our prior would need to be before we would change our action from no action to self-isolation: even if we are somewhat unsure of our prior specification, we may believe that it will be far from this threshold.

d) Sensitivity of the Posterior P⁢(D+|T+) to the Sensitivity and Specificity

  • •

    We may not be certain of the sensitivity and specificity of the test, as these were derived from a test group of finite size (much more on this later in the course!).

  • •

    Alternatively, there may be plans to improve the current test, but in a choice of two ways: method A will modestly improve the sensitivity and method B will modestly improve the specificity. Which method would we suggest?

  • •

    Here we can perform a simple sensitivity analysis by examining the derivative of the posterior with respect to the sensitivity and the specificity, keeping all other things constant when performing the derivative (see partial derivatives in Calculus course):

    Sensitivity:d⁢P⁢(D+|T+)d⁢P⁢(T+|D+)Specificity:d⁢P⁢(D+|T+)d⁢P⁢(T−|D−)

    (note: we may need to rearrange the posterior to perform these derivatives.)

  • •

    For example, denoting the specificity as x=P⁢(T−|D−), then we have

    P⁢(D+|T+) = P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)+(1−x)⁢P⁢(D−)
    d⁢P⁢(D+|T+)d⁢P⁢(T−|D−)=dd⁢x⁢P⁢(D+|T+) = P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)⁢P⁢(D−)[P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)+(1−x)⁢P⁢(D−)]2
  • •

    Check that this yields the value 1.023. The corresponding calculation for the sensitivity would show that the posterior is far more sensitive to improvements in the specificity, and hence we would possibly prefer method B, all things being equal.

e) Odds and the Likelihood Ratio

  • •

    Medical statistics frequently use odds and likelihood ratios as alternative summaries of diagnostic tests.

Definition: Prior and posterior odds and the likelihood ratio

  • •

    Prior odds in favour of A =P⁢(A)P⁢(Ac)

  • •

    Posterior odds in favour of A given B =P⁢(A|B)P⁢(Ac|B).

  • •

    Likelihood ratio for B given A =P⁢(B|A)P⁢(B|Ac)

  • •

    It is simple to show that

    posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. (6)
  • •

    The likelihood ratio can be interpreted as a factor which determines whether the posterior odds are smaller (likelihood ratio <1) or larger (likelihood ratio >1) than the prior odds, and by how much.

2.4 Additional Examples (Not Examinable)

2.4.1 Testing for Down’s Syndrome

Testing for Down’s syndrome in mothers aged 35 from the New England Journal of Medicine.

  • •

    Let D+ be the event that a foetus from a mother aged 35 has Down’s syndrome. We know that P⁢(D+)=1/270 for mothers of this age.

  • •

    The usual test for Down’s syndrome is amnioscentesis, which gives an essentially correct diagnosis. However, it is expensive ($1500) and risky (1/200 chance of miscarriage).

  • •

    An alternative cheap ($75) risk-free blood test is available, however, it is not as accurate as amnioscentesis.

  • •

    Let T+ be the event that the blood test gives a positive indication of Down’s syndrome. The probabilities of various diagnoses are:

    P⁢(T+|D+) =0.89 (sensitivity, correct diagnosis)
    P⁢(T−|D+) =0.11 (false negative)
    P⁢(T+|D−) =0.25 (false positive)
    P⁢(T−|D−) =0.75 (specificity, correct diagnosis)
  • •

    Question: What is the posterior probability of Down’s syndrome given that the blood test came out positive?

Down’s syndrome example: Applying Bayes Theorem

We want P⁢(D+|T+), so as usual use Bayes Theorem:

P⁢(D+|T+) = P⁢(T+|D+)⁢P⁢(D+)P⁢(T+)
= 0.89×1/2700.89×1/270+0.25×269/270
= 0.01306
  • •

    So P⁢(D+|T+)=only ⁢1.3%, even with positive test, so unlikely to actually have a foetus with Down’s syndrome.

  • •

    Exercise: show that P⁢(D+|T−)=1/2000, even with negative test, so still a “fairly high” probability of foetus with Down’s syndrome.

Down’s syndrome example: Odds and the Likelihood Ratio

  • •

    prior odds in favour of Down’s syndrome

    P⁢(D+)1−P⁢(D+)=1269=0.0037.

    The prior odds in favour of no Down’s syndrome, D−, is, inverting, 269:1.

  • •

    posterior odds in favour of Down’s syndrome, given a positive test

    P⁢(D+|T+)1−P⁢(D+|T+)=0.0130.987=0.01323.

    The posterior odds in favour of no Down’s syndrome, D−, is, inverting, about 76:1.

  • •

    When test is positive, it is more likely than before that the foetus has Down’s syndrome, but still quite unlikely

  • •

    likelihood ratio

    L⁢R=P⁢(T+|D+)P⁢(T+|D−)=0.890.25=3.56
  • •

    3.56 times more likely that foetus with Down’s syndrome will lead to a positive test result, than when the foetus does not have Down’s syndrome.

  • •

    check that indeed

    posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio
    0.01323 = 0.0037×3.56

2.4.2 The Prosecutor’s Fallacy

Here is a (slightly modified) extract from the UK Crown Prosecution Service recommendations on interpretation of statistical evidence:

Quotation: UK Crown Prosecution Service

The fallacy is to equate the rarity of the DNA profile to the likelihood of guilt. Expressing the statistical conclusion in the wrong terms may mislead the jury. For example, the scientist’s evidence states:

“The chances of finding the matching profiles if this blood stain had originated from a man in the general population other than and unrelated to the defendant is 1 in 5 million.”

The prosecutor or judge translates this into any of the following statements;

  • •

    the likelihood that the defendant is guilty is 5 million to 1 or;

  • •

    the blood stain is 5 million times more likely to have come from the defendant than any other man;

  • •

    it is 5 million to 1 against that a man other than the defendant left the blood stain.

All the statements in the above paragraph are misleading and require evidence other than the scientist’s finding to support them.

Why are those statements misleading?

Example: Prosecutor’s Fallacy Analysis

  • •

    E = event that the DNA evidence is left

  • •

    G = event that suspect with DNA match is guilty

  • •

    DNA evidence = what is the chance that the DNA at the scene of the crime was left by someone taken at random from the UK population
    = P⁢(E|Gc) (although even this isn’t clear and many books have been written on this subject).

  • •

    The fallacy = confusion of P⁢(E|Gc) with P⁢(G|E)!!
    These are not the same, but are related via Bayes theorem:

    P⁢(G|E)=P⁢(E|G)⁢P⁢(G)P⁢(E|G)⁢P⁢(G)+P⁢(E|Gc)⁢P⁢(Gc).
  • •

    For illustration, let’s assume P⁢(E|G)=1 in which case we know everything except P⁢(G), the prior probability of the suspect’s guilt.

  • •

    Consider what you feel this probability would be if the crime was a burglary near Buckingham palace and there are two suspects with matching DNA

    • –

      a Master Criminal seen in the vicinity

    • –

      the King

  • •

    Suppose P⁢(E|Gc)=1/5⁢m (i.e. 1 in 5 million - and crucially, the same for each of the two suspects)

  • •

    King has P⁢(G)=1/50⁢m (and is innocent),

  • •

    Master criminal has P⁢(G)=1/100

  • •

    What we want to know is P⁢(G|E)

    king: P⁢(G|E) =1/50⁢m1/50⁢m+1/5⁢m×(1−1/50⁢m)=0.0909
    criminal: P⁢(G|E) =1/1001/100+1/5⁢m×99/100=0.99998
  • •

    A fairly extreme example, but it highlights the common confusion between P⁢(E|Gc) and P⁢(G|E), and how they could be very different.
